sentences.text: Dysalotosaurus lacked large thumb spikes and possessed short front limbs with a long tail, adaptations that favored bipedalism over its larger relatives.
A study of bone cross-sectional geometry confirmed that Dysalotosaurus moved on its hind legs with an erect stance.
CT scans of the braincase suggest Dysalotosaurus held its head pointing straight forward when not feeding.
This medium-sized animal featured long hind legs and a tail longer than half its body, which helped it run quickly.
The front of the mouth had a horny beak used for browsing, and it possibly had cheek pouches on the sides.
The name Dysalotosaurus means "hard-to-catch lizard" in Greek and likely refers to the animal's light body.
The species name D. lettowvorbecki honors German officer Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, who served in German East Africa during World War I.
A hemivertebra found in a specimen caused scoliosis, marking the first known evidence of this spinal condition in dinosaurs.
Fossils contain medullary bone tissue, indicating the animal was reproducing.
Bone deformities found in the skeleton represent the oldest known evidence of a viral infection in the scientific record.
The genus Dysalotosaurus was described by Hans Virchow in 1919.
The species Dysalotosaurus was named by Virchow in 1919.
The genus Dysalotosaurus was formally described in 1920 by Josef Pompeckja.
Thousands of bones have been recovered from Tanzania since 1909.
New anatomical information and ontogenetic changes were published in 2026 based on the study of an immature individual from the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania.
Differences in teeth suggest Dysalotosaurus started as an omnivore but became a fully herbivorous adult.
Dysalotosaurus likely lived for about twenty years and lived in herds containing individuals of mixed ages.
The animal reached sexual maturity at approximately ten years of age.
The dinosaur exhibited indeterminate growth with a maximum growth rate comparable to that of a large kangaroo.
Growth accelerated until about 14 years of age, reaching a mass of approximately 60 kilograms.
No fossil eggs or bones of newborn individuals of Dysalotosaurus are known.
In the largest known specimens, neurocentral sutures in the tail were fully closed while others remained open, confirming that growth was not yet complete.
CT scans suggest Dysalotosaurus held its mouth inclined upward at an angle of approximately 17 degrees in its resting position.
The relatively short cochlea indicates a best hearing range of approximately 3500 Hertz.
Dysalotosaurus is included in the family Dryosauridae, a basal group within Iguanodontia.
In 2011, Barrett included Dysalotosaurus with the genera Valdosaurus and Elrhazosaurus in a clade within Dryosauridae based on similarities in the upper metatarsal bones.
Fossils of Dysalotosaurus have been found in Late Jurassic rocks of the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania.
During the Jurassic, the habitat of Dysalotosaurus was a semi-arid coastline of Gondwana featuring tidal flats and lagoons.
Fossils of Dysalotosaurus were found in Late Upper Jurassic rocks of the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania.
Dysalotosaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian stage, between 152.21 and 149.2 million years ago.
In 1977, Peter Galton argued that the similarities between Dysalotosaurus lettowvorbecki and Dryosaurus altus were large enough to justify classifying them in the same genus.
Eventually, Galton considered Dysalotosaurus a junior synonym of Dryosaurus but kept D. lettowvorbecki as a separate species within the genus Dryosaurus.
In 2008, Rauhut and López-Arbarello considered that the assignment of Dysalotosaurus lettowvorbecki to the type of Dryosaurus had not been sufficiently demonstrated.
